title: The Omer: one quality a day
hook: the mystics pair each of the forty-nine days with a quality to refine

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Song of Songs, read in the week of Passover. Your line was the song of songs. Today, the seven weeks from Passover to Shavuot.

Every evening for seven weeks, after nightfall, observant Jews say a blessing and then a number. Today is one day of the Omer. Today is two days. Today is eight days, which is one week and one day. Miss a whole day, and by many rulings you keep counting but stop saying the blessing. Apps, wall charts and little fridge calendars help people keep track. It sounds like the world's most patient countdown. But the mystics turned these forty-nine days into something closer to a training plan.
screen: `A BLESSING, THEN A NUMBER.` → `FORTY-NINE NIGHTS.` → `A COUNTDOWN, OR A TRAINING PLAN?`

segments.voice: Start with the Torah. In Leviticus, from the day the first sheaf of barley is brought, the omer, you count. In the old Jewish translation: "seven weeks shall there be complete." On the fiftieth day comes Shavuot, the feast of weeks. In the rabbis' reading, it's the road from leaving Egypt to receiving the Torah at Sinai: freedom first, then what to do with it. The word for counting is sefirah, and here the mystics come in. In the Kabbalah, a very similar word, sefirot, names the qualities through which God is revealed in the world. The lower seven are usually listed as chesed, loving-kindness; gevurah, strength or restraint; tiferet, beauty and balance; netzach, endurance; hod, humility or splendor; yesod, foundation, the bond between people; and malchut, kingship, presence, the way it all shows up in the world. Seven qualities, seven weeks, and inside each week, seven days. So the first day is loving-kindness within loving-kindness. The second, strength within loving-kindness: love that knows its limits. Forty-nine combinations, one each night. Kabbalists and Hasidic teachers built a practice on it, and many teachers of character, middot, still use it: each day, look at one quality in yourself and refine it a little. Just today's square on the chart. The counting stops being a wait and becomes the preparation. By the time you reach the mountain, you've worked on the person who's arriving.
screen: `SEVEN WEEKS COMPLETE.` · `FROM EGYPT TO SINAI.` · `SEVEN QUALITIES, SEVEN DAYS.` · `ONE SQUARE ON THE CHART.` · then, large: `REFINE ONE QUALITY.`

segments.voice: Choose one quality: kindness, restraint, balance, endurance, humility, connection or presence, maybe the one that's been weakest lately, or too strong. Think of one moment today when it'll be tested, a meeting, a dinner, a drive, and picture meeting it with that quality a little more refined. Just a little.
Sefirah. Counting: the forty-nine days of the Omer, and for the mystics, one quality refined each day. Today's word.
Your line: refine one quality. Forty-nine nights, one square at a time. That's day six hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: From the second night of Passover until Shavuot, observant Jews count the Omer each evening with a blessing, naming the day and week; many also follow the Kabbalistic chart of sefirot, reflecting on one quality each day.

chat.says: Why do some Jews count every night from Passover to Shavuot? Isn't it just a countdown?
options: The Torah says count seven weeks, and mystics gave each day a quality to refine.
It counts down to Rosh Hashanah, the new year, seven weeks away.
It's a seven-week fast, with one meal skipped each evening.

notes: Leviticus 23:15 phrase quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; verify.
Translations of the seven lower sefirot vary (hod as splendor or humility; yesod as foundation or bonding); glosses chosen for a general audience.
Rule on a missed day (continue without a blessing) follows the common Ashkenazi/Sephardi ruling; hedged with 'by many rulings'.
'Sefirah' (counting) and 'sefirot' share a root; the link is presented as one the mystics made, not an etymological claim.
